claim: As of August 8, 2021, the COVID-19 pandemic has caused more than 202.6 million infections and 4.2 million deaths globally.
source: As of August 8, 2021, the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has caused more than 202.6 million infections and 4.2 million deaths globally (Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Dong et al., 2020 as the source for these statistics.

claim: For cases that deteriorate into severe COVID-19, deterioration occurs, on median, 10 days after symptom onset.
source: For cases that deteriorate into severe COVID-19, deterioration occurs, on median, 10 days after symptom onset (Solomon et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Solomon et al., 2020 and Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: Risk factors for severe illness and death include age, sex, smoking, and comorbidities, such as obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.
source: Risk factors for severe illness and death include age, sex, smoking, and comorbidities, such as obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease (Onder et al., 2020; Tartof et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Onder et al., 2020; Tartof et al., 2020; and Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: Age and sex differences in innate, cross-reactive, and adaptive immunity facilitate the higher risks observed in older and male cases.
source: Emerging evidence indicates that age and sex differences in innate, cross-reactive, and adaptive immunity facilitate the higher risks observed in older and male cases (Rydyznski Moderbacher et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2020; Pierce et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rydyznski Moderbacher et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2020; Pierce et al., 2020; and Takahashi et al., 2020.

claim: Robust immune responses putatively mediate nonsevere illness, in part, by controlling the replication of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Conversely, robust immune responses putatively mediate nonsevere illness, in part, by controlling the replication of SARS-CoV-2 (Lucas et al., 2021; Lucas et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lucas et al., 2021 and Lucas et al., 2020, and involves speculative reasoning ('putatively').

claim: URT viral load has been associated with transmission risk, duration of infectiousness, disease severity, and mortality.
source: URT viral load has been associated with transmission risk, duration of infectiousness, disease severity, and mortality (Chen et al., 2021b; Fu et al., 2021; Magleby et al., 2020; Marks et al., 2021; Pujadas et al., 2020; van Kampen et al., 2021; Westblade et al., 2020; Wölfel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Chest computed tomography (CT) evidence of viral pneumonitis suggests pulmonary replication in most symptomatic cases.
source: While chest computed tomography (CT) evidence of viral pneumonitis suggests pulmonary replication in most symptomatic cases (Bernheim et al., 2020), the LRT kinetics of SARS-CoV-2, especially as related to disease severity, remain unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bernheim et al., 2020.

claim: The systematic dataset included 1266 adults and 136 children with COVID-19.
source: The systematic dataset included 1266 adults and 136 children with COVID-19.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section of the abstract and supported by Table 1.

claim: High, persistent LRT shedding of SARS-CoV-2 characterized severe COVID-19 in adults.
source: Our analyses indicated that high, persistent LRT shedding of SARS-CoV-2 characterized severe COVID-19 in adults.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section of the abstract and supported by regression analyses and data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Severe cases tended to show slightly higher URT shedding post-symptom onset, but similar rates of viral clearance, when compared to nonsevere infections.
source: Severe cases tended to show slightly higher URT shedding post-symptom onset, but similar rates of viral clearance, when compared to nonsevere infections.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section of the abstract and supported by regression analyses presented in Figure 2.

claim: After stratifying for disease severity, sex and age (including child vs. adult) were not predictive of respiratory shedding.
source: After stratifying for disease severity, sex and age (including child vs. adult) were not predictive of respiratory shedding.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section of the abstract and supported by stratified regression analyses presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The estimated accuracy for using LRT shedding as a prognostic indicator for COVID-19 severity was up to 81%.
source: The estimated accuracy for using LRT shedding as a prognostic indicator for COVID-19 severity was up to 81%, whereas it was up to 65% for URT shedding.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section of the abstract and supported by distribution analyses and AUC calculations presented in Figure 4.

claim: The estimated accuracy for using URT shedding as a prognostic indicator for COVID-19 severity was up to 65%.
source: The estimated accuracy for using LRT shedding as a prognostic indicator for COVID-19 severity was up to 81%, whereas it was up to 65% for URT shedding.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section of the abstract and supported by distribution analyses and AUC calculations presented in Figure 4.

claim: Disease severity, rather than sex or age, predicts SARS-CoV-2 kinetics.
source: Disease severity, rather than sex or age, predicts SARS-CoV-2 kinetics.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Conclusions section of the abstract and is an inference from the stratified regression analyses.

claim: LRT viral load may prognosticate COVID-19 severity in patients before the timing of deterioration and should do so more accurately than URT viral load.
source: LRT viral load may prognosticate COVID-19 severity in patients before the timing of deterioration and should do so more accurately than URT viral load.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Conclusions section of the abstract and involves inference and speculation based on the prognostic accuracy analyses.

claim: From 1402 COVID-19 cases, 1915 quantitative specimen measurements of SARS-CoV-2 were collected.
source: From 1402 COVID-19 cases, we collected 1915 quantitative specimen measurements (viral RNA concentration in a respiratory specimen) of SARS-CoV-2 (Table 1) and used them to estimate rVLs (viral RNA concentration in the respiratory tract) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: For pediatric cases, the search found only nonsevere infections and URT specimen measurements.
source: For pediatric cases, the search found only nonsevere infections and URT specimen measurements.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1 showing 0 LRT specimens for pediatric cases.

claim: 18 of the 26 contributing studies had low risk of bias according to the modified JBI critical appraisal checklist.
source: Appendix 1—table 1 and Appendix 1—table 2 summarize the characteristics of contributing studies, of which 18 had low risk of bias according to the modified JBI critical appraisal checklist.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and refers to the risk of bias assessment.

claim: For adult COVID-19, the mean URT rVL at 1 DFSO was significantly greater (p = 0.005) for severely infected cases (8.28 [95% CI: 7.71–8.84] log10 copies/ml) than nonsevere ones (7.45 [95% CI: 7.26–7.65] log10 copies/ml).
source: For adult COVID-19, regression analysis showed that the mean URT rVL at 1 DFSO was significantly greater (p = 0.005) for severely infected cases (8.28 [95% CI: 7.71–8.84] log10 copies/ml) than nonsevere ones (7.45 [95% CI: 7.26–7.65] log10 copies/ml) (Figure 2A, D,).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 2.

claim: Severe adult cases tended to clear SARS-CoV-2 from the URT at –0.31 (95% CI: –0.40 to–0.22) log10 copies/ml/day while nonsevere ones did so at –0.28 (95% CI: –0.32 to –0.24) log10 copies/ml/day.
source: Meanwhile, these groups showed comparable URT dynamics post-symptom onset (p for interaction = 0.479), as severe adult cases tended to cleared SARS-CoV-2 from the URT at –0.31 (95% CI: –0.40 to–0.22) log10 copies/ml/day while nonsevere ones did so at –0.28 (95% CI: –0.32 to –0.24) log10 copies/ml/day (Figure 2A, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 2.

claim: For severe cases, the estimated mean duration of URT shedding (down to 0 log10 copies/ml) was 27.5 (95% CI: 21.2–33.8) DFSO.
source: For severe cases, the estimated mean duration of URT shedding (down to 0 log10 copies/ml) was 27.5 (95% CI: 21.2–33.8) DFSO; it was 27.9 (95% CI: 24.4–31.3) DFSO for nonsevere cases.
evidence: The claim is based on extrapolation of regression models to estimate shedding duration.

claim: For nonsevere cases, the estimated mean duration of URT shedding (down to 0 log10 copies/ml) was 27.9 (95% CI: 24.4–31.3) DFSO.
source: For severe cases, the estimated mean duration of URT shedding (down to 0 log10 copies/ml) was 27.5 (95% CI: 21.2–33.8) DFSO; it was 27.9 (95% CI: 24.4–31.3) DFSO for nonsevere cases.
evidence: The claim is based on extrapolation of regression models to estimate shedding duration.

claim: After stratifying adults for disease severity, there were no significant differences in URT shedding levels or dynamics between sex or age groups.
source: After stratifying adults for disease severity, our analyses showed no significant differences in URT shedding levels or dynamics between sex or age groups (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by stratified regression analyses presented in the text and figures.

claim: For severe disease, male and female cases had comparable mean rVLs at 1 DFSO (p = 0.326) and rates of SARS-CoV-2 clearance (p for interaction = 0.280).
source: For severe disease, male and female cases had comparable mean rVLs at 1 DFSO (p = 0.326) and rates of SARS-CoV-2 clearance (p for interaction = 0.280).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results.

claim: For nonsevere illness, male and female cases had no significant difference in mean rVL at 1 DFSO (p = 0.085) or URT dynamics (p for interaction = 0.644).
source: Similarly, for nonsevere illness, male and female cases had no significant difference in mean rVL at 1 DFSO (p = 0.085) or URT dynamics (p for interaction = 0.644).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results.

claim: For nonsevere illness, younger and older adults had no significant difference in URT shedding levels at 1 DFSO (p = 0.294) or post-symptom onset dynamics (p for interaction = 0.100).
source: For nonsevere illness, younger and older adults had no significant difference in URT shedding levels at 1 DFSO (p = 0.294) or post-symptom onset dynamics (p for interaction = 0.100).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results.

claim: For severe disease, younger and older adult age groups showed similar mean rVLs at 1 DFSO (p = 0.915) and rates of viral clearance (p for interaction = 0.359).
source: For severe disease, the adult age groups showed similar mean rVLs at 1 DFSO (p = 0.915) and rates of viral clearance (p for interaction = 0.359).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results.

claim: For pediatric COVID-19, the mean URT rVL at 1 DFSO was 7.32 (95% CI: 6.78–7.86) log10 copies/ml.
source: For pediatric COVID-19, regression estimated that, in the URT, the mean rVL at 1 DFSO was 7.32 (95% CI: 6.78–7.86) log10 copies/ml and the SARS-CoV-2 clearance rate was –0.32 (95% CI: –0.42 to –0.22) log10 copies/ml/day (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 2.

claim: For pediatric COVID-19, the SARS-CoV-2 clearance rate in the URT was –0.32 (95% CI: –0.42 to –0.22) log10 copies/ml/day.
source: For pediatric COVID-19, regression estimated that, in the URT, the mean rVL at 1 DFSO was 7.32 (95% CI: 6.78–7.86) log10 copies/ml and the SARS-CoV-2 clearance rate was –0.32 (95% CI: –0.42 to –0.22) log10 copies/ml/day (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 2.

claim: The estimated mean duration of URT shedding (down to 0 log10 copies/ml) was 22.6 (95% CI: 17.0–28.1) DFSO for children with COVID-19.
source: The estimated mean duration of URT shedding (down to 0 log10 copies/ml) was 22.6 (95% CI: 17.0–28.1) DFSO for children with COVID-19.
evidence: The claim is based on extrapolation of regression models to estimate shedding duration.

claim: Between pediatric cases with nonsevere illness and adults with nonsevere illness, both URT shedding at 1 DFSO (p = 0.653) and URT dynamics (p for interaction = 0.400) were similar.
source: Between pediatric cases, who had nonsevere illness in our dataset, and adults with nonsevere illness, both URT shedding at 1 DFSO (p = 0.653) and URT dynamics (p for interaction = 0.400) were similar (Figure 2B, F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 2.

claim: URT shedding at 1 DFSO was greater for severely affected adults when compared to children with nonsevere disease (p = 0.017), but URT dynamics remained similar (p for interaction = 0.863).
source: In contrast, URT shedding at 1 DFSO was greater for severely affected adults when compared to children with nonsevere disease (p = 0.017), but URT dynamics remained similar (p for interaction = 0.863) (Figure 2C, F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 2.

claim: At 4 DFSO, the mean rVL in the LRT of severe cases (8.42 [95% CI: 7.67–9.17] log10 copies/ml) was significantly greater (p = 0.006) than that of nonsevere cases (6.82 [95% CI: 5.95–7.69] log10 copies/ml).
source: At the initial day in our analyzed period (4 DFSO), the mean rVL in the LRT of severe cases (8.42 [95% CI: 7.67–9.17] log10 copies/ml) was significantly greater (p = 0.006) than that of nonsevere cases (6.82 [95% CI: 5.95–7.69] log10 copies/ml) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: Severe cases had persistent LRT shedding, with no significant trend in SARS-CoV-2 clearance up to 10 DFSO (–0.14 [95% CI: –0.32–0.030] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.105).
source: Nonetheless, severe cases had persistent LRT shedding, with no significant trend in SARS-CoV-2 clearance up to 10 DFSO (–0.14 [95% CI: –0.32–0.030] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.105), whereas nonsevere cases rapidly cleared the virus from the LRT (–0.41 [95% CI: –0.64 to –0.19] log10 copies/ml/day, p < 0.001) (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: Nonsevere cases rapidly cleared the virus from the LRT (–0.41 [95% CI: –0.64 to –0.19] log10 copies/ml/day, p < 0.001).
source: Nonetheless, severe cases had persistent LRT shedding, with no significant trend in SARS-CoV-2 clearance up to 10 DFSO (–0.14 [95% CI: –0.32–0.030] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.105), whereas nonsevere cases rapidly cleared the virus from the LRT (–0.41 [95% CI: –0.64 to –0.19] log10 copies/ml/day, p < 0.001) (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: For nonsevere cases, the estimated mean duration of LRT shedding (down to 0 log10 copies/ml) was 20.4 (95% CI: 13.2–27.7) DFSO.

claim: For severe COVID-19, younger and older adults had comparable mean LRT rVLs at 4 DFSO (p = 0.745).
source: For severe COVID-19, regression analysis showed comparable mean LRT rVLs at 4 DFSO between younger and older adults (p = 0.745) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: For severe cases, younger adults had no significant trend in LRT SARS-CoV-2 clearance (–0.20 [95% CI: –0.32 to 0.042] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.105).
source: For severe cases, both age groups also had persistent LRT shedding in the analyzed period: younger adults (–0.20 [95% CI: –0.32 to 0.042] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.105) and older adults (–0.13 [95% CI: –0.39 to 0.13] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.316) both had no significant trend in SARS-CoV-2 clearance (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and figures.

claim: For severe cases, older adults had no significant trend in LRT SARS-CoV-2 clearance (–0.13 [95% CI: –0.39 to 0.13] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.316).
source: For severe cases, both age groups also had persistent LRT shedding in the analyzed period: younger adults (–0.20 [95% CI: –0.32 to 0.042] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.105) and older adults (–0.13 [95% CI: –0.39 to 0.13] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.316) both had no significant trend in SARS-CoV-2 clearance (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and figures.

claim: Severely affected male cases had no significant trend in LRT shedding (0.001 [95% CI: –0.16 to 0.19] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.988).
source: Likewise, severely affected male cases had no significant trend in LRT shedding (0.001 [95% CI: –0.16 to 0.19] log10 copies/ml/day, p = 0.988) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nonsevere cases showed similar SARS-CoV-2 shedding between the URT and LRT.
source: Interestingly, nonsevere cases showed similar SARS-CoV-2 shedding between the URT and LRT (Figure 3B), whereas severe cases shed greater and longer in the LRT than in the URT (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of regression analyses presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: Severe cases shed greater and longer in the LRT than in the URT.
source: Interestingly, nonsevere cases showed similar SARS-CoV-2 shedding between the URT and LRT (Figure 3B), whereas severe cases shed greater and longer in the LRT than in the URT (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of regression analyses presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: At 4 DFSO, the URT rVL of nonsevere adults was 6.62 (95% CI: 6.50–6.74) log10 copies/ml, which was not different from the LRT rVL of nonsevere adults (p = 0.651).
source: At 4 DFSO, the URT rVL of nonsevere adults was 6.62 (95% CI: 6.50–6.74) log10 copies/ml, which was not different from the LRT rVL of nonsevere adults (p = 0.651).

claim: For severe adults, the rVL at 4 DFSO was significantly lower in the URT (7.34 [95% CI: 7.01–7.68] log10 copies/ml) than the LRT (p = 0.031).
source: Conversely, for severe adults, the rVL at 4 DFSO was significantly lower in the URT (7.34 [95% CI: 7.01–7.68] log10 copies/ml) than the LRT (p = 0.031) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis results presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: Both severe and nonsevere adult COVID-19 showed broad variation in URT shedding throughout disease course.
source: While regression analyses compared mean shedding levels and dynamics, we fitted rVLs to Weibull distributions to assess the heterogeneity in rVL. Both severe and nonsevere adult COVID-19 showed broad variation in URT shedding throughout disease course (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by distribution analyses presented in the text and Figure 4A.

claim: For severe disease, the standard deviation (SD) of URT rVL was 1.86, 2.34, 1.89, and 1.90 log10 copies/ml at 2, 4, 7, and 10 DFSO, respectively.
source: For severe disease, the standard deviation (SD) of rVL was 1.86, 2.34, 1.89, and 1.90 log10 copies/ml at 2, 4, 7, and 10 DFSO, respectively.

claim: For nonsevere illness, the standard deviation of URT rVL was 2.08, 1.90, 1.89, and 1.96 log10 copies/ml at 2, 4, 7, and 10 DFSO, respectively.
source: For nonsevere illness, these SDs were 2.08, 1.90, 1.89, and 1.96 log10 copies/ml, respectively.

source: Notably, our distribution analyses indicated that the top 2–9% of adults with COVID-19 harbored 80% of the SARS-CoV-2 copies in the URT on each DFSO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: The claim is based on cumulative distribution analyses presented in the text and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distributions of severe and nonsevere LRT shedding bifurcated along disease course.
source: In contrast, the distributions of severe and nonsevere LRT shedding bifurcated along disease course (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by distribution analyses presented in the text and Figure 4E.

claim: At 6 DFSO, the estimate at the 80th case percentile of LRT rVL was 9.40 (95% CI: 8.67–10.20) log10 copies/ml for severe COVID-19, while it was 7.66 (95% CI: 6.65–8.83) log10 copies/ml for nonsevere illness.
source: At 6 DFSO, the estimate at the 80th case percentile of LRT rVL was 9.40 (95% CI: 8.67–10.20) log10 copies/ml for severe COVID-19, while it was 7.66 (95% CI: 6.65–8.83) log10 copies/ml for nonsevere illness.
evidence: The claim is based on distribution analyses of the data.

source: At 10 DFSO, the difference between 80th case percentile estimates expanded, as they were 8.63 (95% CI: 8.04–9.26) and 6.01 (95% CI: 4.65–7.78) log10 copies/ml for severe and nonsevere disease, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on distribution analyses of the data.

claim: Nonsevere illness was associated with greater skewing in LRT shedding than severe disease in the analyzed period.
source: Furthermore, our data indicated that nonsevere illness was associated with greater skewing in LRT shedding than severe disease in the analyzed period (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by distribution analyses presented in the text and Figure 4E.

claim: For nonsevere COVID-19, the SD of LRT rVL was 1.92, 2.01, and 2.09 log10 copies/ml at 6, 8, and 10 DFSO, respectively.
source: For nonsevere COVID-19, the SD of rVL was 1.92, 2.01, and 2.09 log10 copies/ml at 6, 8, and 10 DFSO, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on distribution analyses of the data.

claim: For severe disease, the SD of LRT rVL was 1.25, 1.37, and 1.61 log10 copies/ml for 6, 8, and 10 DFSO, respectively.

evidence: The claim is based on distribution analyses of the data.

claim: On each DFSO, the top 2–12% of cases harbored 80% of the LRT copies of SARS-CoV-2 for adults with nonsevere COVID-19.
source: On each DFSO, the top 2–12% of cases harbored 80% of the LRT copies of SARS-CoV-2 for adults with nonsevere COVID-19, whereas it was the top 10–20% of cases for adults with severe disease (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, E to H).
evidence: The claim is based on cumulative distribution analyses presented in the text and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: On each DFSO, the top 10–20% of cases harbored 80% of the LRT copies of SARS-CoV-2 for adults with severe disease.
source: On each DFSO, the top 2–12% of cases harbored 80% of the LRT copies of SARS-CoV-2 for adults with nonsevere COVID-19, whereas it was the top 10–20% of cases for adults with severe disease (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, E to H).
evidence: The claim is based on cumulative distribution analyses presented in the text and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 5 DFSO, the estimated specificity was 93.3% and the estimated sensitivity was 64.4% at a prognostic threshold of 9.10 log10 copies/ml for LRT shedding.
source: For example, at 5 DFSO, the estimated specificity was 93.3% and the estimated sensitivity was 64.4% at a prognostic threshold of 9.10 log10 copies/ml (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on cumulative distribution analyses presented in the text and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

source: For 8 DFSO, the estimated specificity and sensitivity was 73.1% and 88.8%, respectively, at a prognostic threshold of 5.95 log10 copies/ml.

claim: LRT shedding more accurately predicts COVID-19 severity than does URT shedding.
source: Taken together, our data indicated that LRT shedding more accurately predicts COVID-19 severity than does URT shedding.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the prognostic accuracy analyses comparing URT and LRT.

claim: Adults with severe COVID-19 showed slightly higher rVLs shortly after symptom onset in the URT, but similar SARS-CoV-2 clearance rates, when compared with their nonsevere counterparts.
source: In the URT, we found that adults with severe COVID-19 showed slightly higher rVLs shortly after symptom onset, but similar SARS-CoV-2 clearance rates, when compared with their nonsevere counterparts.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from regression analyses presented earlier in the Results section.

claim: Sex and age had nonsignificant effects on SARS-CoV-2 shedding after stratifying for disease severity.
source: After stratifying for disease severity, our analyses showed that sex and age had nonsignificant effects on SARS-CoV-2 shedding for each included analysis (summarized in Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from stratified regression analyses.

claim: While sex and age influence the tendency to develop severe COVID-19, there is no such sex dimorphism or age distinction in shedding among cases of similar severity.
source: Thus, while sex and age influence the tendency to develop severe COVID-19 (Onder et al., 2020; Tartof et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020), we find no such sex dimorphism or age distinction in shedding among cases of similar severity.
evidence: The claim combines established knowledge (cited) with findings from the current study's analyses.

claim: Children with nonsevere illness show similar URT shedding post-symptom onset as adults with nonsevere illness.
source: This includes children, who had nonsevere illness in our study and show similar URT shedding post-symptom onset as adults with nonsevere illness.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analyses comparing pediatric and adult cases.

claim: High, persistent LRT shedding of SARS-CoV-2 characterizes severe COVID-19 in adults.
source: Notably, our analyses indicate that high, persistent LRT shedding of SARS-CoV-2 characterizes severe COVID-19 in adults.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from LRT regression analyses.

claim: Previous reports have found prolonged LRT shedding for weeks in critically ill adult patients.
source: Previous reports have found prolonged LRT shedding for weeks in critically ill adult patients (Buetti et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buetti et al., 2020 and Huang et al., 2020.

claim: A severity-associated difference in both shedding and clearance in the LRT begins, at least, at 4 DFSO.
source: They reveal a severity-associated difference in both shedding and clearance in the LRT which begins, at least, at 4 DFSO; our dataset had limited LRT samples before 4 DFSO.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analyses of LRT data and acknowledges data limitations.

claim: Severe disease is associated with higher rVLs in the LRT than the URT throughout the analyzed period, whereas nonsevere illness shows similar shedding between the LRT and URT.
source: Interestingly, our analyses also reveal an early bifurcation between the LRT and URT for severe COVID-19. That is, severe disease is associated with higher rVLs in the LRT than the URT throughout the analyzed period, whereas nonsevere illness shows similar shedding between the LRT and URT.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of regression analyses between LRT and URT.

claim: The effective immune responses associated with milder COVID-19 do not significantly inhibit early, or prolonged, SARS-CoV-2 replication in the LRT of severely affected adults.
source: This suggests that the effective immune responses associated with milder COVID-19, including innate, cross-reactive, and coordinated adaptive immunity (Lucas et al., 2020; Rydyznski Moderbacher et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2020; Pierce et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2020), do not significantly inhibit early, or prolonged, SARS-CoV-2 replication in the LRT of severely affected adults.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the LRT shedding data combined with cited knowledge about immune responses.

claim: Poorly controlled LRT replication tends to continue, at least, to 10 DFSO, which coincides with the timing of clinical deterioration (median, 10 DFSO).
source: Hence, poorly controlled LRT replication tends to continue, at least, to 10 DFSO, which coincides with the timing of clinical deterioration (median, 10 DFSO) (Solomon et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
